content: This document is designed to provide detailed guidance to WHO Member States and personnel from non-State actor organizations involved in any aspect of clinical trials. This includes activities such as planning, conducting, analyzing, overseeing, interpreting, and funding clinical trials aimed at evaluating the effects of health interventions for any purpose in any setting. It also applies to those responsible for educating others about clinical trials. The scope of this guidance encompasses all clinical trial designs, with a particular emphasis on randomized clinical trials (RCTs). These include comparisons of two or more interventions, whether blinded or unblinded, and whether conducted in parallel, cluster, crossover, factorial, adaptive platform, decentralized, or other designs. The health interventions covered include, but are not limited to, the administration of pharmaceutical medicines, biological products such as cells and vaccines, surgical or radiological procedures, diagnostics, medical devices, nutritional measures, cognitive and psychological interventions, supportive or preventive care, physical therapy, digital and public health approaches, traditional or herbal remedies, and screening processes. These interventions may be novel or pre-existing but used in a new way (e.g., repurposed or optimized) or aimed at gaining further knowledge about current practices. The guidance applies to clinical trials conducted for any purpose, including generating evidence for guideline development, clinical practice recommendations, public health strategies, and health technology assessments. It is relevant to any geographical, economic, or societal context, including trials conducted in hospitals, primary care, or community settings, or where interventions are delivered directly to participants. The document is intended for all roles involved in clinical trials, including researchers, clinicians, patient and public groups (including trial participants), regulators, ethics committees, institutional review boards, research funders, and trial sponsors (academic, governmental, nonprofit, and commercial). It emphasizes the importance of considering local, national, or regional contextual factors and regulations, and encourages collaboration with local patient groups and affected communities to ensure appropriate adaptation and compliance with universal scientific and ethical standards. This guidance complements existing documents to support the implementation of universal ethical and scientific standards in clinical trials, with a focus on under-represented populations. It does not represent a legal standard and does not override existing guidance. It shares principles with guidelines from the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH), including ICH E8(R1), ICH E6(R3), and ICH E9, as well as other recent guidance documents such as those from the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS) and the Good Clinical Trials Collaborative (GCTC). These sources have been adapted as needed for this document. For clinical trials intended to support regulatory submissions for medicinal products, sponsors should also refer to ICH guidelines and any relevant guidance issued by the regulatory authorities to which they plan to submit. However, the scope of this WHO guidance is not limited to medicinal products or trials conducted for regulatory approval. The development of this guidance was overseen by the WHO Technical Advisory Group (TAG) for the Development of Best Practices for Clinical Trials. The initial draft was prepared by Vasee Moorthy and Christina Reith, drawing from existing CIOMS and GCTC guidance. Feedback from the TAG was incorporated into a revised draft, which underwent public consultation from July to September 2023. The WHO Secretariat disseminated the draft to regional offices, technical programs, professional networks, non-State actors, and other key stakeholders. A total of 179 responses from 48 countries were received, with input from academic stakeholders, NGOs, and national health or regulatory authorities. Additional consultations were held with private sector representatives and Member States, and a global stakeholder survey was conducted in August 2023 to identify barriers to conducting clinical trials and propose priority actions. Nearly 3,000 participants worldwide responded to the survey. Outcomes from the survey were discussed in in-person consultations held in various global locations, attended by approximately 300 experts and stakeholders. These consultations provided further input for the draft guidance. The final guidance, prepared by Vasee Moorthy and Christina Reith, integrated all received feedback. A TAG meeting in April 2023 reviewed the final draft before its submission for executive clearance and publication. Declarations of interest were collected from all TAG members and publicly disclosed. Clinical research is essential for addressing public health challenges. It spans five key areas: measuring the magnitude and distribution of health problems, understanding their causes, developing interventions, implementing solutions, and evaluating their impact. Clinical studies are broadly categorized into non-interventional (observational) and interventional (clinical trials). Observational studies compare health outcomes between individuals exposed to a factor and those not exposed, without predetermined allocation. In contrast, interventional studies (clinical trials) evaluate the effects of prospectively assigning subjects to one or more interventions on health outcomes. Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) are a key type of interventional study, involving randomization to allocate participants to different intervention arms. RCTs may involve individual or group allocation (e.g., cluster RCTs) and are particularly valuable for comparing interventions. However, some trials, such as early-phase or single-arm trials, do not involve randomization. Clinical trial interventions may include pharmaceutical medicines, biological products, vaccines, surgical or radiological procedures, diagnostics, medical devices, nutritional measures, cognitive and psychological interventions, supportive or preventive care, physical therapy, digital and public health approaches, traditional or herbal remedies, and screening processes. These interventions may be novel or repurposed and may include placebos or comparators. Clinical trials can be conducted at any level of the health system, from home and community settings to intensive care units. Beyond traditional parallel-group RCTs, other trial designs include crossover, factorial, adaptive, and platform trials. Platform trials, for example, allow simultaneous evaluation of multiple interventions using master protocols and can adapt based on accumulating data. They were pivotal in generating evidence for COVID-19 therapeutics. Decentralized and point-of-care trials are increasingly used, addressing critical questions in clinical care settings rather than specialized research environments. All clinical trials should aim to resolve uncertainties about the effects of health interventions, with results informing decisions on development, evaluation, regulatory licensing, clinical guidelines, and health policy.
